section_summary: This section documents the attempted bombing of the Japanese steamship Hiyu Maru at Seattle and subsequent Japanese and Canadian inquiries. It also contains consular reports on Japanese shipping, shipbuilding and maritime policy in 1938, with particular attention to whether Japanese authorities were steering cargo toward Japanese vessels. The section ends partway through a longer report on shipping during June 1938.

subfiles.title: Treasury filing or routing fragment
subfiles.about: A fragment records routing and filing information for a Treasury communication.
subfiles.summary: Only filing marks and an office heading remain.

subfiles.title: Coast Guard dispatch on attempted bombing of Hiyu Maru
subfiles.to: Coast Guard Headquarters, for Bureau of Customs Investigation Unit
subfiles.about: Seattle authorities report an alleged plot to bomb the Japanese ship Hiyu Maru.
subfiles.summary: The dispatch describes Forsyth’s drowning, Partridge’s arrest and statements, recovered equipment, and a search for a submerged bomb. Partridge alleged connections to Chinese consulates, but the investigation was still in progress.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Japanese Embassy counselor about Hiyu Maru
subfiles.about: Suma thanks Seattle police and requests precautions for Japanese ships in American ports.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton explains that port precautions chiefly fall to local authorities. Suma says Japanese reporting now suggests the plot was an individual act without outside direction.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Suma conversation to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department forwards its February 1 memorandum about the Hiyu Maru bombing attempt.
subfiles.summary: Cover instruction enclosing the Suma–Hamilton conversation.

subfiles.title: Ottawa letter on Canadian inquiry into Hiyu Maru plot
subfiles.about: The Legation relays Canada’s response to Japanese inquiries into the Seattle bombing plot.
subfiles.summary: Skelton says Canada’s investigation is incomplete and promises to share its final report. A postscript describes Japanese war pamphlets found in Canadian Pacific tourist folders.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Queries Ottawa On Bombing Plot
subfiles.about: Japan asks Canada for details of the alleged bombing attempt by two Canadians.
subfiles.summary: Reports Japanese representations and continuing Canadian inquiries.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Canadian Legation counselor about Hiyu Maru
subfiles.about: Riddell asks whether the United States can help Canada answer Japan’s inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton and Hickerson recount the initial Treasury report and Suma’s visit. They say the Department has no further useful information and suggest Canadian authorities consult Seattle police.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Riddell conversation to Ottawa
subfiles.about: The Department forwards its February 3 conversation with the Canadian Legation.
subfiles.summary: Cover instruction enclosing the Riddell conversation.

subfiles.title: Navy transmittal of Japanese consul’s request
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards Virginia correspondence concerning protection of Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Transmits two letters from Virginia and the Japanese consul.

subfiles.title: Virginia adjutant general’s letter to Navy
subfiles.about: Waller encloses the Japanese consul’s appeal and relays Governor Price’s cooperative response.
subfiles.summary: Virginia’s governor supports maintaining friendly relations with Japan.

subfiles.title: Japanese consul’s request to protect ships in Virginia
subfiles.about: Wakasugi asks Virginia to safeguard Japanese ships and crews in its harbors.
subfiles.summary: Requests precautionary measures against threats to Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During January 1938
subfiles.from: William E. Yuni, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: A monthly survey covers Japanese shipbuilding, ports, policy, services, trade and fleet distribution.
subfiles.summary: The report notes a decline in shipbuilding orders and tonnage under construction, while describing new freighters and whalers, harbor and dockyard proposals, and revived China routes. It discusses a proposal to reserve Japanese cargo for Japanese vessels, a projected China shipping company, freight negotiations, falling cargoes and labor changes. Tables give construction and fleet distribution figures, followed by sources.

subfiles.title: Confidential note on Japanese shipping difficulties in Siam
subfiles.about: Shipping company representatives report boycotts and uncertain cargo handling in Siam.
subfiles.summary: Chinese residents’ boycotts reportedly disrupt Japanese schedules and sales.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting evidence of Japanese cargo policy
subfiles.about: The Department asks for evidence that Japan is carrying out a Japanese-vessels-only cargo policy.
subfiles.summary: Requests prompt updates on the proposal described in Kobe’s January report.

subfiles.title: Second conversation with Suma about Hiyu Maru
subfiles.about: Suma reports the accused accomplice’s acquittal and praises American port precautions.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton reiterates that American port authorities work to maintain order and prevent unlawful acts against Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding second Suma conversation
subfiles.about: The Department forwards the April 8 conversation about the Hiyu Maru case.
subfiles.summary: Cover instruction enclosing the second Suma conversation.

subfiles.title: Department note on Kobe shipping inquiry
subfiles.about: A file note summarizes Kobe’s findings on Japanese cargo preferences and rebates.
subfiles.summary: Foreign lines reportedly lose cargo; government pressure remains suspected but unproved.

subfiles.title: Kobe inquiry into transportation of Japanese goods
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Kobe interviews foreign shipping agents about alleged preference for Japanese vessels.
subfiles.summary: Agents report falling foreign cargoes and widespread secret rebates by Japanese lines, but offer no concrete proof of a formal government policy. Some suspect informal pressure, exclusion from shipping arrangements, and disregard of importers’ requests for foreign carriers. A postal official describes use of Japanese ships as national policy.

subfiles.title: Department note on Tokyo despatch 2870
subfiles.about: A file note flags a short Tokyo despatch on Japanese-vessel policy.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to examine the despatch in full.

subfiles.title: Tokyo despatch on Japanese-vessel cargo policy
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports inquiries into whether Japan adopted a Japanese-vessels-only cargo policy.
subfiles.summary: Embassy inquiries find no evidence of adoption or imminent adoption; Grew characterizes the proposal as shipping-industry wishful thinking.

subfiles.title: Osaka consular inquiry into Japanese-vessel policy
subfiles.from: George N. Naxinson, American Consul General
subfiles.about: The Osaka consulate checks whether Japanese cargo is being reserved for Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Informal inquiries find no implementing steps. Murata reportedly advocated the idea publicly, but without a practical plan.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum forwarding Taihoku report
subfiles.from: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Cameron forwards the Taihoku consul’s response on Japanese-vessel policy.
subfiles.summary: Encloses Warner’s April 1 confidential communication.

subfiles.title: Taihoku report on local shipping policy
subfiles.about: Warner reports local encouragement of Japanese shipping and effects of exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: The policy is informal; exchange controls hinder foreign chartering. American port-call figures are supplied.

subfiles.title: Yokohama inquiry into Japanese-vessel policy
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Boyce asks foreign shipping interests whether the Japanese government is directing cargo to Japanese lines.
subfiles.summary: He finds no evidence of an official plan and attributes Dollar Line losses to other factors.

subfiles.title: Department note on Boyce’s follow-up
subfiles.about: A file note points to Boyce’s indications of government influence on cargo routing.
subfiles.summary: Notes suggestive reports while emphasizing the absence of definite proof.

subfiles.title: Boyce’s follow-up on Japanese cargo routing
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Boyce forwards Dollar Line reports concerning wood pulp and truck shipments.
subfiles.summary: The reports suggest that import approvals and yen payments may favor Japanese carriers. Boyce regards them as indications of possible indirect government influence, not definite proof.

subfiles.title: Dollar Line report on wood pulp imports
subfiles.from: N. V. Carlson, Yokohama freight office
subfiles.about: The Yokohama office reports wood pulp import limits and advice to buy on FOB terms.
subfiles.summary: Government approvals could steer freight and payments toward Japanese lines.

subfiles.title: Dollar Line report on Diamond T trucks
subfiles.from: N. V. Carlson, Yokohama freight office
subfiles.about: The office investigates the routing of truck chassis ordered for a Mukden company.
subfiles.summary: The purchaser booked Japanese shipping before ordering; the office explores possible alternative routing.

subfiles.title: Nagoya shipping figures for American ports
subfiles.from: C. H. Stephan, American Vice Consul, Nagoya
subfiles.about: Stephan supplies ship and cargo counts relevant to the Japanese-vessel policy inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Reports first-quarter Nagoya sailings and cargo by vessel nationality.

subfiles.title: Shipping in the Japanese Empire During June 1938
subfiles.about: The report surveys June shipbuilding, port works, China shipping policy and foreign-exchange proposals.
subfiles.summary: The report lists new orders, ships under construction and June launchings, including a new whaler. It describes a Filipino ship built in Japan, repairs to the Asama Maru, and proposed Japanese dockyard expansion at Shanghai. Its shipping-policy discussion covers a projected China company, proposals to increase foreign-exchange income through shipping, and the beginning of a section on coastal fisheries. The report continues beyond page 160.
